summary_plain: The Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE) burned gaseous fuels like methane and ethylene in microgravity on the International Space Station. By observing how these flames detach and stabilize away from burners, researchers aim to improve combustion efficiency and reduce soot. Understanding flame stability in space directly enhances spacecraft fire safety.
summary_expert: The SLICE investigation studied the structure, stabilization mechanisms, and liftoff limits of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity. Testing was conducted using exchangeable burner tubes, a fan-driven flow duct, and fuels including methane, ethylene, and nitrogen-diluted mixtures. The apparatus captured high-resolution images across multiple testing experiments to correlate flame structure and stability with flow dynamics, burner diameter, coflow velocity, and fuel composition.

key_findings.text: The SLICE investigation utilized the SPICE hardware in the space station glovebox to study lifted and lifting flames, starting and completing operations in 2012.
Exploratory tests for SLICE were conducted in 2009 on the ISS as part of the Smoke Point In Coflow experiment to examine lifted flame behavior under increasing coflow velocity.
The SLICE apparatus captured more than 4,000 high-resolution images across 13 testing experiments using a fan-driven flow duct and exchangeable burner tubes.

earth_applications: Cleaner and more efficient engines and industrial burners
